passage: The night before the maths test, ten-year-old Yogesh left his book shut and watched cartoons. "I didn't even study," he told everyone at school the next day, cheerfully. When his mark came back low, he shrugged: "See? I didn't try." But his stomach hurt, and he had not learned the chapter. At fifteen, before the district cricket match, Yogesh stayed up until two playing a game. His friend Varun asked, "Aren't you playing tomorrow?" Yogesh waved a hand. "It's fine." He dropped two catches the next day and lost by a few runs, and he said in the pavilion, "I was so tired. If I'd slept, we would have won." Varun said nothing, though he had been waiting for a proper partner all season. At twenty, Yogesh let a term paper wait until the last night. By dawn he had a rough draft, and told his classmate Bhupen, "It's just a rush job. Don't judge it." When the grade was middling, he said it proved nothing about him. Yet the paper was on a subject he loved, and he never learned whether he could have done it well.

qa.q: What did Yogesh watch the night before the maths test?
qa.a: He watched cartoons.

qa.q: How is Yogesh's protecting himself the same at ten, fifteen and twenty, and what does it cost?
qa.a: At ten he skipped studying, at fifteen he stayed up gaming before the match, and at twenty he waited until the last night for the paper. Each time he had a ready excuse for a poor result, but he lost the real chance to learn or win.

qa.q: What was Yogesh feeling when he said he had not tried after the low mark?
qa.a: He felt hurt and afraid of looking unintelligent, as his aching stomach shows.

qa.q: What could Yogesh do differently before his next paper?
qa.a: He could start early with a small first step and give the paper a fair try so the result tells him about his ability.

grounding: The same person protects himself with an excuse at three ages: not studying, staying up before a match, and leaving a paper to the last night.

passage: At nine, Yusuf pushed a spoonful of bitter gourd around his plate. "It was expensive," his mother Arohi had said, so he made himself finish it, feeling ill. At another time he kept playing a dull board game for an hour and a half, because he had already spent an hour on it. At fifteen, he sat in an evening coaching class for chemistry that he hated, and could not follow. His parents had paid the fees for two years and the fees for the third were due. "If I leave now, all that money is wasted," he said, and he went again, tired. His marks did not improve, and his weekends disappeared. At twenty, Yusuf was in the second year of a commerce degree that no longer fit him. He was drawn to marine biology, but leaving would make the earlier years feel wasted. His friend Hansa asked one afternoon, "If you were starting today, knowing what you know, would you choose this?" He was quiet a long time. "No," he said, and looked out at the rain, stunned to hear it aloud.

qa.q: What food did Yusuf make himself finish at nine?
qa.a: He made himself finish the bitter gourd.

qa.q: What is the same about Yusuf's reasons for continuing at nine, fifteen and twenty?
qa.a: At nine he kept eating and playing because of the money and hour already spent, at fifteen he stayed in the coaching class because of the fees paid, and at twenty he stayed in the degree because leaving would make the earlier years feel wasted. Each time past effort decided what he did next.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when he said no to Hansa's question?
qa.a: He felt stunned and quietly relieved to say it aloud, after years of pushing on.

qa.q: What could Yusuf do next to choose his future rather than his past?
qa.a: He could learn what marine biology courses need, talk to Hansa or a counsellor, and decide by asking what he wants from now on.

grounding: The same person lets past investment decide at three ages: finishing food and a game, staying in a hated class, and staying in a degree that no longer fits.

passage: At ten, Rajni stood in the crowd at the school fair as the tug-of-war began. Everyone screamed, so she screamed too and pushed forward with the others until someone's slipper flew off. She couldn't remember deciding to push. At fifteen, a classmate's video went round the class and dozens of comments piled up beneath it, all jokes at her expense. Rajni typed one of her own, because everyone had, and saw it get five hearts. Later she saw the classmate's face at her desk, and her stomach sank. She deleted her comment that evening and told the class teacher Vishal the next morning, who spoke to the whole class about it that day and asked the comments to be taken down. At twenty, Rajni stood in the stadium among thousands, chanting louder than she ever would alone. When a surge began near the gate, she felt the crowd carry her forward and shouted with it. Then her friend Kunal caught her sleeve. "Let's get out to the side." They edged out together and stood breathing by the wall.

qa.q: What did Rajni delete on the evening after typing it?
qa.a: She deleted her comment.

qa.q: How does Rajni's part in a crowd at ten, fifteen and twenty share a pattern?
qa.a: At ten she pushed with the others without deciding to, at fifteen she added a comment because everyone had, and at twenty she chanted louder than she would alone and was carried by the surge. Each time the crowd's energy made her personal responsibility fade until something, like a face or a friend's hand, pulled her back.

qa.q: What was Rajni feeling when she saw the classmate's face at her desk?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and guilty, as her sinking stomach shows, realising the target had seen every word.

qa.q: What could Rajni do next time she notices herself swept along in a crowd?
qa.a: She could pause and ask herself whether she would do it alone, and step out to the side with a friend if things turn unsafe.

grounding: The same person is swept along at three ages: shouting and pushing at a fair, adding to an online pile-on, and being carried by a stadium crowd until a friend pulls her out.

passage: On a spring afternoon, nine-year-old Farhan planted a bean seed in a cracked cup with his grandfather Baljeet. He watered it each morning and turned it toward the window. On the seventh day, a pale green loop pushed up through the soil. "I did that," Farhan whispered, and he ran to show everyone. Another week, he fixed the wheel of his toy truck with a bent paper clip, and it rolled again. He began to notice that when he tried something, things changed. At fifteen, his family moved cities after his father's job ended, and money was tight and tempers short. Farhan could not stop the arguments. His cousin Simran said, "Make two lists: what's yours to change, and what isn't." That night he wrote: study every day, ask the maths teacher for help, talk to Simran on Sundays, keep the room tidy. On the other side: father's job, the moving, other people's moods. He took the first list to school on Monday. It did not solve everything, but he felt his feet under him.

qa.q: What did Farhan plant with his grandfather?
qa.a: He planted a bean seed.

qa.q: How does Farhan's sense of influence at nine connect to what he does at fifteen?
qa.a: At nine planting the seed and fixing the truck showed him that his actions changed things, and at fifteen he used that belief to list what was his to change, like studying and asking for help, and what was not, like his father's job. Acting on the first list gave him power in a hard time.

qa.q: What was Farhan feeling when he saw the pale green loop push up through the soil?
qa.a: He felt proud and amazed, because it showed him that his effort had made something happen.

qa.q: What could Farhan do if he feels helpless again about things outside his control?
qa.a: He could go back to his list, choose one small step from it, and keep talking to Simran about how he feels.

grounding: The same person builds agency at two ages: a child who sees results from planting a seed and mending a toy, and a teenager who lists what he can influence in a hard family situation.

passage: At sixteen, Kalyani's friend Santosh pointed at his cousin's motorbike. "Come on, three of us fit. It's only ten minutes." Kalyani shook her head. "No, I'm taking the bus. Want to get tea after?" He rolled his eyes. "My mother tracks my location anyway," she added, which was partly true, and they laughed. But by the next week he was asking again, and again, and calling her boring. Kalyani felt her resolve wobble. She told her aunt Rukmini, who said, "Good friends accept a no. Would you like me to talk with him, or would you rather do it yourself?" Kalyani chose to talk to him alone. Nine years later, Kalyani and Santosh were partners in a small bakery. He wanted to buy a costly oven at once, while she wanted to wait a year. Voices rose. Then she said, "We both want the shop to last. Let's rent an oven for three months and see. If it works, we buy, and I'll happily agree that you were right about needing one." Santosh let out a laugh. "Three months. Deal."

qa.q: What did Kalyani suggest to Santosh instead of the motorbike?
qa.a: She said she was taking the bus and asked if he wanted tea afterwards.

qa.q: How is Kalyani's way of handling disagreement at sixteen linked to her way at twenty-five?
qa.a: At sixteen she shook her head, said she was taking the bus, asked about tea and told her aunt Rukmini when Santosh kept asking. At twenty-five, when voices rose over the oven, she said they both wanted the shop to last and offered to rent an oven for three months and see.

qa.q: What was Kalyani feeling when Santosh kept asking again and calling her boring?
qa.a: She felt pressured and unsure of herself, and her resolve wobbled.

qa.q: What could Kalyani do if Santosh keeps pressuring her about risky things?
qa.a: She can tell Rukmini again, keep saying no, and spend more time with friends who accept a refusal.

grounding: The same person handles persuasion at two ages: resisting peer pressure toward a risky ride at sixteen, and proposing a trial rental as a face-saving compromise with a business partner at twenty-five.

passage: At five, Sunaina sat on the floor beside her grandmother Lakshmi while the evening puja began. The brass lamp was lit, the bell rang, and the smell of camphor drifted up. Sunaina watched the flame turn in circles. She clapped along with the aarti and asked, "Why do you swing the light, Nani?" Lakshmi smiled. "Because it's a way of saying thank you, and everyone joins in." Sunaina held up her palms to the warmth of the flame and copied her grandmother. At twenty, Sunaina stood on a street in the late afternoon as a wedding procession came down it. Drummers marched, dancers spun, and a groom sat on a decorated horse. Her friend Aditi, whose cousin was the groom, waved to her from the crowd. "Come, walk with us!" Sunaina stepped aside to let the drummers pass, and asked quietly, "What does the song they are playing mean? I don't want to do anything wrong." Aditi grinned. "It's the welcome song. Just clap along and smile." Sunaina clapped, happy to belong, and asked one more question when the music stopped.

qa.q: What did Sunaina ask her grandmother about the light?
qa.a: She asked why Lakshmi swings the light.

qa.q: How does Sunaina's reading of ritual differ at five and at twenty?
qa.a: At five she copied her grandmother's clapping and asked why the light is swung, learning that actions mark special moments. At twenty she read the wedding procession of drummers, dancers and a groom on a horse as joy, and asked Aditi what the song meant before joining.

qa.q: What was Sunaina feeling when she asked about the song at the procession?
qa.a: She felt respectful and a little unsure, wanting to join without doing anything wrong.

qa.q: What could Sunaina do at another community's ceremony where she does not know the customs?
qa.a: She could watch what others do and ask a friend like Aditi quietly what things mean and how to take part respectfully.

grounding: The same person reads collective rituals at two ages: a child learning from an evening puja what marks a special moment, and a young adult reading and asking about a wedding procession.
